metadata.title: CIS Kubernetes Benchmark — Security Best Practices

entries.description: Every Pod must define a restrictive SecurityContext. Pod-level: runAsNonRoot: true, runAsUser: 1001, runAsGroup: 1001, fsGroup: 1001, seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault. Container-level: allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, capabilities.drop: [ALL]. Mount emptyDir for /tmp if read-only filesystem is set.
decision_rules: Apply both pod-level and container-level SecurityContext — they are complementary
Use seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault to restrict system calls
Mount emptyDir volumes at paths that require write access (e.g. /tmp)
tradeoffs: readOnlyRootFilesystem may break applications that write to the container filesystem — identify and mount emptyDir for those paths
anti_patterns: Setting allowPrivilegeEscalation: true or omitting it (defaults to true without explicit false)
aws_alignment: EKS enforces Pod Security Standards — set namespace labels pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted

entries.description: Create a dedicated ServiceAccount per application with automountServiceAccountToken: false. Define a Role with only required verbs on required resources. Bind via RoleBinding. Do not grant access to secrets unless strictly necessary.
decision_rules: Create a dedicated ServiceAccount for each workload — never use the default ServiceAccount
Set automountServiceAccountToken: false on ServiceAccount to prevent token auto-mounting
Grant only required verbs (get, list) on required resources — never use wildcard (*)
tradeoffs: Fine-grained RBAC requires understanding of which API resources each workload actually accesses
anti_patterns: Using the default ServiceAccount for application workloads
Granting cluster-admin or wildcard permissions to application ServiceAccounts
Adding secrets to the Role resource list without justification
aws_alignment: Map to EKS IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) for AWS API access from pods

entries.description: Apply a default-deny-all NetworkPolicy in each namespace (podSelector: {}, policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]). Then add explicit allow policies per service. Example: allow Ingress from ingress-nginx namespace on port 8000 only for pods matching app=api.
decision_rules: Start with a default-deny-all policy in every namespace
Add explicit ingress and egress allow rules only for required traffic paths
Use namespaceSelector for cross-namespace traffic (e.g. allowing ingress controller)
tradeoffs: NetworkPolicy requires a CNI plugin that supports it (Calico, Cilium, Weave) — does not work with Flannel alone
anti_patterns: Operating namespaces with no NetworkPolicy (all traffic allowed by default)
Using podSelector: {} in allow policies without scoping by policyTypes
aws_alignment: Use VPC CNI with Calico on EKS for NetworkPolicy enforcement
Complement with Security Groups for Pods on EKS for L4 controls

entries.concept: Secrets management with External Secrets Operator (CIS 5.4)
entries.description: Use External Secrets Operator (ESO) or Sealed Secrets instead of plain Kubernetes Secret manifests. ESO ExternalSecret references a SecretStore (e.g. vault-backend) and syncs secrets into a Kubernetes Secret. ConfigMaps should hold only non-sensitive configuration.
decision_rules: Never commit plain Kubernetes Secret manifests with base64-encoded values to version control
Use External Secrets Operator to sync from AWS Secrets Manager, Vault, or GCP Secret Manager
Use ConfigMaps exclusively for non-sensitive configuration (APP_ENV, LOG_LEVEL)
tradeoffs: ESO adds operational complexity — requires installing the controller and configuring SecretStore
Sealed Secrets is simpler but less flexible — secrets can only be decrypted by the cluster
anti_patterns: Storing database URLs or passwords in ConfigMaps (not encrypted at rest)
Committing Kubernetes Secrets with real credentials to git repositories
aws_alignment: Use ESO with AWS Secrets Manager provider on EKS
Use Secrets Store CSI Driver with AWS SSM Parameter Store as an alternative

entries.description: Every container must define both resources.requests and resources.limits. Example: requests memory 128Mi cpu 100m, limits memory 512Mi cpu 500m. Without limits, a single pod can starve other workloads on the node.
decision_rules: Define both requests (scheduler hint) and limits (enforcement) for every container
Use LimitRange objects to enforce defaults for namespaces missing explicit resource declarations
tradeoffs: Limits that are too tight cause OOMKilled events or CPU throttling — profile workloads before setting values
anti_patterns: Deploying containers with no resource limits to shared cluster nodes
Setting limits without requests — scheduler cannot make optimal placement decisions
aws_alignment: EKS node autoscaling (Karpenter) uses requests to pack pods onto nodes efficiently

entries.concept: Liveness and Readiness probes for workload health
entries.description: Define livenessProbe (restarts unhealthy pods: httpGet /health, initialDelaySeconds 15, periodSeconds 20, failureThreshold 3) and readinessProbe (removes unhealthy pods from Service endpoints: httpGet /ready, initialDelaySeconds 5, periodSeconds 10) for every container.
decision_rules: Use readinessProbe to control traffic routing — pod is only added to Service endpoints when ready
Use livenessProbe to restart pods stuck in an unrecoverable state
Set startupProbe for slow-starting applications to prevent premature liveness failures
tradeoffs: Overly aggressive liveness probes (short timeouts, low failureThreshold) cause unnecessary restarts
Missing readiness probes cause traffic to be sent to not-yet-ready pods
anti_patterns: Using the same endpoint and thresholds for both liveness and readiness probes
Not defining any health probes — Kubernetes cannot detect application-level failures

entries.concept: Pod Disruption Budget for high availability
entries.description: A PodDisruptionBudget (PDB) limits voluntary disruptions (node drains, rolling updates). Example: minAvailable: 2 with selector app=api ensures at least 2 pods remain available during node maintenance.
decision_rules: Create a PDB for every production Deployment with more than 1 replica
Use minAvailable (absolute) or maxUnavailable (percentage) depending on SLO requirements
tradeoffs: PDB with minAvailable equal to replicas will block node drains — leave at least 1 pod drainable
anti_patterns: Deploying multi-replica workloads without a PDB — all pods may be disrupted simultaneously
Setting minAvailable: 0 — defeats the purpose of the PDB
aws_alignment: PDB works with EKS Managed Node Groups during node version upgrades

entries.description: Configure Ingress with TLS using cert-manager (cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod). Annotations: ssl-redirect: true, force-ssl-redirect: true. TLS spec references a Secret containing the certificate. All HTTP traffic redirected to HTTPS at the ingress level.
decision_rules: Always terminate TLS at the Ingress — never expose plain HTTP to the internet
Use cert-manager with Let's Encrypt for automated certificate provisioning and renewal
Set nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: true to enforce HTTPS
tradeoffs: Let's Encrypt rate limits apply — use staging issuer for testing
Certificate renewal requires outbound internet access from the cluster for ACME challenges
anti_patterns: Exposing services over HTTP in production
Using self-signed certificates without a trust chain (causes browser/client warnings)
aws_alignment: Alternatively use AWS ALB Ingress Controller with ACM certificates on EKS
